text: Ramifications are the knock-on effects of something — the further results that spread out from one event, often ones nobody planned. The word comes from a Latin root meaning branch, so picture one thing splitting into many. Burials from 7,000 years ago have ramifications today because those bodies are now coming out of the ground and causing arguments about land, money and who gets to live where.

To thrive is to do more than survive — to grow strong and do well. A plant thrives in good soil; a team thrives with a good coach. Saying the Chinchorro culture thrived 7,000 years ago means these people were not barely hanging on: they lived successfully on that coast for thousands of years.

A ritual is a set of actions done the same careful way every time, usually because a group treats them as important or sacred. Blowing out birthday candles is a small ritual. The Chinchorro burial rituals were huge ones: months of exact steps for preparing a dead body, repeated the same way for thousands of years.

A mummy is a dead body whose soft parts have been kept from rotting away, so skin and hair are still there thousands of years later. Most people think of Egypt, but the Chinchorro of South America were doing it about 2,000 years earlier. To mummify a body is to treat it on purpose so it lasts.

The Atacama is a long strip of desert down the Pacific coast of South America, across northern Chile and southern Peru. It is famous for being the driest non-polar desert on Earth — some weather stations there have gone years without measuring any rain. That dryness is the reason the bodies buried in it never rotted.

The Chinchorro were a people who lived along that desert coast from about 7000BC to 1000BC, feeding themselves by hunting and fishing. They are known today for one thing above all: they made the oldest mummies anyone has found. The name is also used for the modern Chilean agency, Chinchorro Marka, that now looks after their sites.

BC stands for Before Christ, the way people label years that came before the year 1. BC years count backwards, so 7000BC is far older than 1000BC — about 9,000 years ago versus 3,000. Saying the Chinchorro lived from 7000BC to 1000BC means their way of life lasted roughly 6,000 years.

Meticulous means extremely careful about small details, doing a job slowly and thoroughly so nothing is missed. Calling the Chinchorro meticulous preservers of their dead is high praise for people with stone tools: their mummification took months of exact, fiddly work, taking a body apart, drying it and rebuilding it.

To preserve something is to keep it from rotting, breaking or being lost. It is the same idea as preserving fruit in a jar, just applied to bodies and to ancient sites. Preservers are the people doing the preserving — here, the Chinchorro themselves, and later the museum experts who tried to keep the mummies safe.

To do something with no regard for a thing is to ignore it completely when deciding. Social status means how important or powerful a person counts as in their society — rich or poor, chief or ordinary. Saying the Chinchorro mummified people with no regard for social status means it did not matter who you were: almost everybody got the same treatment, which was unusual in the ancient world.

To do something deliberately is to do it on purpose, after thinking about it — the opposite of by accident. That single word is what makes these bodies special. Plenty of ancient corpses survived by luck, dried out or frozen by chance, but the Chinchorro chose to preserve theirs, which is why they count as the world's oldest deliberately preserved bodies.

Numerous just means many, in large numbers. It shares a root with number. The odd twist in this story is that the mummies are so numerous they have become a problem: normally archaeologists want more of something rare, but here there are more bodies than Chile has room to keep.

An archaeologist studies people of the past by digging up and examining the physical things they left behind — tools, rubbish heaps, buildings, bones. It is a different job from a historian, who mostly reads what people wrote. For a culture like the Chinchorro, which left no writing at all, archaeologists are the only way we know anything.

An agency here is not a place that books holidays. It means an official organisation set up by a government to handle one particular job. Chinchorro Marka is that kind of agency: Chile's government created it and gave it one task, looking after the country's Chinchorro sites.

If you are charged with a task, you have been given the responsibility for it — it is now officially your job. This is a different meaning from being charged with a crime, and different again from charging a phone. The agency was charged with the protection of the sites, so protecting them is what it exists to do.

To stumble upon something is to find it completely by chance, without looking for it. Nobody actually trips over; the phrase just borrows the idea of an accidental step. The archaeologist stumbled upon a skeleton while walking around the town, which tells you how close to the surface these bodies now are.

As a noun, remains means what is left of a dead body — bones, and sometimes preserved skin. It is a quieter, more respectful word than corpse, which is why archaeologists and news reports use it. Watch out for the everyday verb, as in the problem remains, which means something quite different.

To expose something is to uncover it so it is out in the open, no longer protected. Wind and rain expose the mummies by stripping away the soil above them. That is bad news here, because once a body is exposed to sunlight, heat and air it starts to fall apart after surviving for thousands of years underground.

The prefix re means again, so reburying is simply burying something a second time. It sounds like giving up, but it is a deliberate choice: soil blocks light and holds a steady temperature, so the ground is the best storage box anyone has. Researchers study a body where it lies and then cover it again.

A phenomenon is something that happens and can be observed, especially something notable enough to need explaining. Lightning is a natural phenomenon; a song everyone suddenly plays is a cultural one. Saying bodies coming out of the ground is not a new phenomenon means it has been happening for over a century, not just now.

Issuing from a place means coming out of it steadily, like smoke issuing from a chimney. This is not the school office issuing you a laptop, though both come from the idea of something going out. Mummies have been issuing from the ground since the early 1900s, meaning they keep appearing, year after year.

An expedition is an organised trip made for a purpose, usually to somewhere remote or hard to reach — exploring, climbing, or in this case collecting scientific finds. It takes planning, a team and supplies, which is what separates it from an ordinary journey. Expeditions in 1917 carried the first Chinchorro mummies off to museums.

To excavate is to dig something out of the ground carefully. An excavation is one such dig. Archaeologists do not just shovel: they scrape away thin layers, record exactly where each object sat, and photograph everything, because where a thing was found tells them almost as much as the thing itself.

Erosion is the slow wearing away of land by wind, water or ice, which carries the loosened material somewhere else. It is what carves valleys and eats away at beaches. In the Atacama, strong winds blow the dry soil off the burial ground bit by bit, and each layer removed brings more mummies closer to the surface.

To accelerate is to speed up. A car accelerates when the driver presses the pedal; a process accelerates when it starts happening faster than before. The bodies were always going to surface eventually, but stronger winds and more people tramping about are accelerating it, so it is happening faster than anyone can cope with.

An anthropologist studies human beings and their societies — how groups of people live, what they believe, how their bodies and cultures differ. Archaeology is really one branch of it that works through dug-up objects. Veronica Silva is quoted here because studying human remains is part of that job.

Keen means eager or enthusiastic about something. It appears twice here, and the second time is the interesting one: saying the fishing families are not so keen is a very British, very understated way of saying they do not want to move at all. Keen can also mean sharp, as in a keen blade or a keen sense of smell.

In situ is Latin for in its place, and scientists use it to mean studying something exactly where it was found instead of taking it away. Because museums have no room and moving a fragile mummy risks wrecking it, researchers now work in situ: they examine the body in the ground, then cover it back up.

UNESCO is a branch of the United Nations that deals with education, science and culture. Its best-known job is keeping the World Heritage list. It owns nothing and has no police force — it works by persuading, advising and paying, while the country itself stays in charge of the site.

A World Heritage site is a place UNESCO has judged so important that losing it would be a loss for all of humanity — the Pyramids of Giza and the Great Barrier Reef are on the list. Being added does not hand the place to UNESCO; the country keeps control and promises to protect it, gaining expert help, money and a great deal of attention. That attention is exactly what caused trouble here.

A landscape is a whole stretch of country seen together — the hills, the coast, the valleys, not a single spot. UNESCO listed the Chinchorro remains and their landscape, meaning the protection covers the land around the bodies too, not just the bodies. That wider boundary is why a fishing village a short walk away is caught up in the rules.

Something makeshift is thrown together quickly from whatever is at hand, standing in for the proper version. It is usually not meant to last, though it often does anyway. The fishing families' homes are makeshift because they were built fast from scrap, without permission or plans, which is part of why the site's protectors object to them.

To relocate is to move to a different place to live or work. The re prefix means again and locate means to place, so it is literally to place yourself again somewhere else. UNESCO would like the families to relocate, which is a polite word for a hard thing: leaving the homes and the fishing spot they already have.

A mayor is the elected head of a town or city's government, in charge of local matters like roads, rubbish and permits. Because voters choose the mayor, a mayor is expected to speak up for local people. That is exactly what Christian Zavala is doing when he complains the mummies get more attention than the living residents do.

Tension here does not mean a rope being pulled tight. It means the strained, uneasy feeling between people who disagree and might soon clash. To up the tension is to make that feeling worse. The mayor upped it by publicly taking one side in the argument between the archaeologists and the village.

A politician's constituents are the ordinary people who live in the area they were elected to represent — whether or not those people actually voted for them. The word shows up constantly in news about elections and government, so it is worth knowing. The mayor is saying his constituents, the living people of his district, are being ignored in favour of bodies that are 7,000 years old.

To exhibit something is to put it on display in public, the way a museum exhibits paintings or a school exhibits science projects. A place where that happens is an exhibition. The hoped-for new centre would let the mummies be both studied by researchers and exhibited to visitors in the same building.

To collaborate is to work together on something as partners. Doing it in collaboration with a group means they are genuinely involved in the work, not just told about it afterwards. That word is the whole point of the last paragraph: the plan only works if the people of Camarones are partners in it rather than an obstacle to it.

Residents are the people who actually live in a place, as opposed to tourists who are only passing through. The whole argument in this story is between residents and visitors: the archaeologists want tourists to come and pay, while the residents want somewhere to live and a way to earn money.

Arica is a coastal city in the far north of Chile, close to the border with Peru and right in the driest part of the Atacama. It is the nearest sizeable city to the Chinchorro burial grounds, which is why the museums and the new building project are based around it.

Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, sitting in the middle of the country's long north to south strip, roughly 2,000km south of the desert. The big national museums are there, which is where mummies were sent for study in the past — and part of why moving them is such a long haul now.

Caleta Camarones is a tiny fishing settlement on the Chilean coast near Arica, sitting in the Camarones valley. Caleta is Spanish for a small cove, and camarones means shrimp. It matters here because it sits inside the protected Chinchorro site: the same ground holds the mummies and the people's homes.
